# Exercise Gal209: Fixed Fields Generated by Torsion Coordinates

## Problem Statement

> [!question] Original Exercise 7.5.3
> (a) Show that the map $\theta$ is a homomorphism.
>
> (b) Consider the set $\{f_0^d:d\in(\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z-0)/\{\pm1\}\}$ and the field containments
> $$
> \mathbb C(X(1))\subset\mathbb C(j,\{f_0^d\})\subset\mathbb C(X_1(N))\subset\mathbb C(X(N)).
> $$
> Show that since $f_0^d\circ\gamma=f_0^{(0,d)\gamma}$ for $\gamma\in\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)$, the fixing subgroup in $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)/\{\pm I\}\Gamma(N)$ of $\mathbb C(j,\{f_0^d\})$ is $\{\pm I\}\Gamma_1(N)/\{\pm I\}\Gamma(N)$, and thus $\mathbb C(X_1(N))=\mathbb C(j,\{f_0^d\})$ and (7.9) holds.
>
> (c) Similarly, show that
> $$
> f_0\circ\gamma=\sum_{\delta=1}^{N-1} f_0^{\delta(c,d)},\qquad\gamma=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\in\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z),
> $$
> i.e., this is the sum of the $x$-coordinates of the nonzero points of the $N$-cyclic subgroup of $E_{j(\tau)}$ generated by either point with $x$-coordinate $f_0^{(c,d)}(\tau)$. We already know $f_0\in\mathbb C(X_0(N))$. Use Exercise 7.5.1(c) to show that, if $\gamma\notin\Gamma_0(N)$, then $f_0$ and $f_0\circ\gamma$ take different values at the cusp $\Gamma(N)\infty$ of $X(N)$. Thus $\mathbb C(X_0(N))=\mathbb C(j,f_0)$ and (7.10) holds. Also show that $j_N(\gamma\tau)=j(\gamma'(N\tau))$, where
> $$
> \gamma'=\begin{pmatrix}N&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\gamma\begin{pmatrix}1/N&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},
> $$
> and consequently $\mathbb C(X_0(N))=\mathbb C(j,j_N)$. (A hint for this exercise is at the end of the book.)

> **Context and notation.** The functions are $f_0^d=f_0^{(0,d)}$, $f_1=f_0^1$, $f_0=\sum_{d=1}^{N-1}f_0^d$, and $j_N(\tau)=j(N\tau)$, with $N>1$. The map $\theta$ is pullback $f\mapsto f\circ\gamma$ on $\mathbb C(X(N))$. The source hint for (c) uses the cusp at infinity and the lattice-sum limit; all equalities of fields are inside this modular-function field.

## Hints

> [!hint]- Hint 1
> Fixing all nonzero multiples of the second basis vector can be tested on the vector $(0,1)$.

> [!hint]- Hint 2
> For part (c), put $g=\gcd(c,N)$ and sum the cusp limits. The resulting limit is $3(g^2-N)/2$.

## Solution

> [!success]- Solution
> **Proof provenance:** Independent derivation. Imported results are named at their point of use.
>
> (a) The book composes automorphisms as right exponents: $f^{\sigma\sigma'}=(f^\sigma)^{\sigma'}$. Define $f^{\theta\gamma}=f\circ\gamma$. Then
> $$
> f^{\theta\gamma\,\theta\gamma'}=(f\circ\gamma)\circ\gamma'=f\circ(\gamma\gamma')=f^{\theta(\gamma\gamma')}.
> $$
> This proves the homomorphism with that composition convention. With ordinary left composition of operators, pullback is contravariant and the same formula is an antihomomorphism; the fixed fields are identical.
>
> (b) On a nonsingular Weierstrass cubic, $x(U)=x(V)$ if and only if $V=\pm U$. Equality of $f_0^{v}$ and $f_0^w$ therefore means $w=\pm v$ modulo $N$: evaluate at a generic $\tau$, for which the analytic $N$-torsion identification is an isomorphism. In particular fixing $f_0^1$ means $(0,1)\gamma=\pm(0,1)$ modulo $N$, equivalently $c=0$ and $d=\pm1$ modulo $N$. The determinant then gives $a=d$ modulo $N$. This is precisely $\{\pm I\}\Gamma_1(N)$. Such a matrix fixes every $f_0^d$, and conversely fixing all of them fixes $d=1$. Galois correspondence in the finite modular-function extension now proves both the indicated equality and
> $$
> \mathbb C(X_1(N))=\mathbb C(j,f_1),\qquad f_1=f_0^1,
> $$
> which is (7.9).
>
> (c) Sum the transformation law of Exercise 7.5.1 over $\delta$. Set $g=\gcd(c,N)$. Exactly the $g-1$ indices $\delta=kN/g$, $1\le k<g$, satisfy $\delta c=0$ modulo $N$. Since $\gcd(c,d)=1$, multiplication by $d$ permutes the nonzero residue classes modulo $g$. The limits proved there, including $g_2/g_3\to9/(2\pi^2)$, give
> $$
> \lim_{\tau\to i\infty}f_0(\gamma\tau)
> =-\frac32(N-1)+\frac92\sum_{k=1}^{g-1}\csc^2(\pi k/g)
> =\frac32(g^2-N).
> $$
> Here $\sum_{k=1}^{g-1}\csc^2(\pi k/g)=(g^2-1)/3$, obtained by differentiating $\sum_{k=0}^{g-1}\cot(z+\pi k/g)=g\cot(gz)$ and comparing constant terms as $z\to0$. For $\gamma\in\Gamma_0(N)$ the value is $3N(N-1)/2$; otherwise $g<N$, so the value differs. Thus the stabilizer of $f_0$ in the modular Galois group is exactly the image of $\Gamma_0(N)$. Galois correspondence gives $\mathbb C(X_0(N))=\mathbb C(j,f_0)$, or (7.10).
>
> Let $A=\operatorname{diag}(N,1)$. The identity $A\gamma\tau=(A\gamma A^{-1})(N\tau)$ proves the formula for $\gamma'$. If $\gamma\in\Gamma_0(N)$, then $\gamma'=\begin{pmatrix}a&Nb\\c/N&d\end{pmatrix}\in\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)$ and $j_N\circ\gamma=j_N$.
>
> Conversely suppose $j_N\circ\gamma=j_N$. Choose $z=N\tau\in\mathcal H$ transcendental over $\mathbb Q$. Since $j$ classifies complex elliptic curves, $j(\gamma'z)=j(z)$ implies $\gamma'z=\delta z$ for some $\delta\in\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)$. If the rational Möbius transformations $\gamma'$ and $\delta$ differed, their equality at $z$ would give a nonzero quadratic polynomial over $\mathbb Q$ satisfied by $z$. Thus they agree projectively; their determinants are one, so $\gamma'=\pm\delta$. In particular $c/N$ is integral, hence $\gamma\in\Gamma_0(N)$. This is the exact stabilizer and proves $\mathbb C(j,j_N)=\mathbb C(X_0(N))$.
